newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS-Haywire Venezuelan money markets puzzle many.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Haywire Venezuelan money markets puzzle many.

text.p: Bizarre goings-on in Venezuela's financial markets have left the government and market-watchers stumped, with only one clue to go on: new foreign ownership of the country's once-troubled banks.
Increased lending, a bouncing bolivar and haywire interbank lending rates are just some of the signs of newly aggressive banking by the country's freshly privatized banks, traders and analysts said.
Venezuela's Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar was not acting coy when he promised an investigation into the recent weird behavior of Venezuelan money markets.
"It strikes me as strange that the Central Bank has been obliged ... to drain (excess) liquidity, even as the financial system shows signs of illiquidity," Matos said.
"We have to rigorously analyze why that is so."

Matos put his finger on the apparent paradox. Even as the Central Bank has aggressively mopped-up excess liquidity, interbank lending rates -- showing every sign of illiquidity -- have gyrated between 10 and 90 percent since late May.
Furthermore, the long dormant market now turns over more than 50 billion bolivars ($103 million) daily.
Analysts and traders say the new-found volatility is due to a profound, one-off structural change in Venezuela's financial system: sharp banking by now-private banks.
"Large banks are changing the way their treasuries work," said one interbank trader.

"When they were state-owned, they just used to sit on their spare cash. Now they actively manage it for their clients: lend it out, borrow on it, change it into dollars and back to bolivars," he added.
Analysts say a large part of the problem is simply money spread unevenly around the system.
Three of the countries five largest banks hold 40 percent of the country's 5.3 trillion bolivars of deposits between them, according to Softline financial consultants.

Provincial, now run by Spain's Banco Bilbao de Vizcaya, is the country's largest. Banco de Venezuela, bought by Banco Santander late last year, is the third biggest, and Banco Consolidado, now run by Chile's Infisa, is the country's fifth.
"They used to just sleep on their cash," local Santander economist Ricardo Penfold said.

No more. Moreover, there is a lot of cash in the system to play with. Labor reforms and public sector pay rises have pushed budgeted government spending this year up 30 percent to 10.2 trillion bolivars ($21.1 billion) -- cash that will soon be floating through the economy.
"That's around 5.9 percent of gross domestic product, or 40 percent of existing liquidity (in the financial system)," Metroeconomica analyst Jose Barcia said.

Such a huge injection of money threatens the government's year-end inflation target of 30 percent. Yet, despite the excess liquidity, interbank lending rates continue to hop and soar, while turnover on the long dormant market now tops 50 billion bolivars ($103 million) daily.
"It strikes me as strange that the Central Bank has been obliged ... to drain (excess) liquidity, even as the financial system shows signs of illiquidity," Finance Minister Matos said Thursday.
"We have to rigorously analyze why that is so."

Another reason for recent market volatility, analysts say, are fears the government may have to devalue to fund labor reform spending next year. Devaluations increase bolivar revenues from Venezuela's largely dollar-denominated oil exports.
As banks and companies switch to dollars on devaluation worries, bolivar liquidity dries up and interbank lending rates shoot up. That in turn prompts investors to switch back into bolivars.
Similarly aggressive banking can be found in newly-launched television campaigns to court new depositors.

Banco de Venezuela -- television motif: an elephant dancing the cha-cha-cha -- and Banco Provincial -- featuring a more traditional hoarding pig -- now offer holidays, televisions and cars as lottery prizes for new depositors.
Lending is also soaring, rising nine percent in March and seven percent in April.

The new client-oriented approach stands in stark contrast to the 1994-5 banking crisis, that saw half the financial system fold, when depositors had to offer large minimum balances to open a new account and pay high maintenance fees.
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
